goal: Build a two-week study plan for my linear algebra final covering eigenvalues, diagonalization, and orthogonality.

turns.text: My linear algebra final is in two weeks and I need a study plan. The exam covers eigenvalues, diagonalization, orthogonal projections, and least squares.

Two weeks is workable. Week one: eigenvalues and diagonalization, with practice problems daily. Week two: orthogonality and least squares, plus two full past papers. Which topic feels weakest right now?
Diagonalization for sure. Also, what's the best way to take notes while doing practice problems? I feel like my notes are a mess.
For problem-solving courses, keep an error log rather than traditional notes: every mistake goes in with the wrong step and the correction. It's more useful for revision than rewriting theory.
An error log is interesting. Should I keep it in a physical notebook or an app? I've been trying to pick a note app for months, like Notion versus Obsidian.
Notion is easier to start with; Obsidian is better for linked, long-term notes. Obsidian stores plain markdown files locally, which some people prefer for ownership of their data.
Ooh linked notes sounds like the zettelkasten thing. Is zettelkasten actually useful or is it just a productivity fad?

Zettelkasten shines for research and writing, where connecting ideas over years pays off. For most people it becomes procrastination dressed up as organization — the system matters less than the reviewing.
That's such a good point about productivity systems being procrastination. I watch so many productivity videos and never actually do the thing. Why is watching productivity content so addictive?

It gives the feeling of progress without the discomfort of the actual work — planning is dopamine-cheap, doing is dopamine-expensive. Watching someone organize their life feels adjacent to organizing yours.
Dopamine-cheap versus dopamine-expensive is so real. Is the whole dopamine detox trend legit science or another internet myth?

The pop version is oversimplified — you can't deplete or reset dopamine like a meter. But the underlying practice of removing high-stimulation habits for a while does help recalibrate what feels rewarding.
Makes sense. My phone is definitely the high-stimulation habit. What are the best settings changes to make a phone less addictive, like grayscale mode?
Grayscale helps some people, but removing home-screen icons for social apps, turning off all non-human notifications, and moving the phone out of your bedroom have bigger measured effects.
The bedroom one is hard because my phone is my alarm. What alarm clock would you recommend, ideally one of those sunrise light ones?
Sunrise alarms like the Philips SmartSleep or the Hatch Restore are the popular picks — the light ramps up over 30 minutes before the sound, which makes winter mornings noticeably easier.
The Hatch one looks nice. Does it work with smart home stuff? My roommate has been building out a Home Assistant setup and keeps adding devices.

Hatch's integration story is weak — there's no official API, though the community has reverse-engineered parts of it for Home Assistant. If deep integration matters, a smart bulb plus a regular alarm is more flexible.
Interesting, maybe we could rig a smart bulb sunrise alarm with Home Assistant automations then. What hardware does a basic Home Assistant setup need to run?

A Raspberry Pi 4 or a small mini-PC is the usual base, plus a Zigbee USB stick if you want to control bulbs and sensors directly without each brand's cloud. From there automations are all YAML or the visual editor.
